items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: if you said an artist is Sammy Davis Jr. Check to see his demeanor and manner.

ctx.x: That’s another thing I wanted to ask you about. The concept, the difference between, as we know it today with pop culture, the difference between an artist and an entertainer. Because when I look at some of the earlier great jazz musicians, to me they were both. What they did it was art, it was beautiful, it was so beautifully constructed, and yet it was entertaining. And now it seems like we have entertainers that get paid exorbitant amounts of money to sing or play about things that don’t have much merit. There…

Well it’s a little more sophisticated. And I think lazy people don’t like jazz because they don’t want to take the time to really find out anything about it. How can I address that? Well it made me think of one thing, and I’ll come back to your question. But one time I had to deal with sidemen versus artists. Or getting sidemen to look at themselves like artists. Sidemen might be just a person like myself. I was in a big band and I got a chance to play solos here and there. I became aware of the difference…

You know Madonna was signed to a contract for 60 million dollars here about a year ago. And I don’t begrudge people their success, but I, when, you know I’ve won some cultural grants. And whenever I won a grant, at the end of the grant period I have to fill out all these things about how I spent the money and what I did and how it helped the community and what kind of people it reached and who I hired. items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I think I’ve done some things with Sammy Davis Jr. and so forth.

ctx.x: And Basie himself, I hope I’ve learned something from him so far as how to take a natural thing and make it saleable. Because it was so natural for him to say one more time on the end, but that sold it as much as the music did. Because at the end he says “one more time” and we play it all over again. Now this, I remember, we did a movie with Jerry Lewis, “Cinderfella.” And this little creative bit that Basie did on it made this

usable to many things. I think I’ve done some things with Sammy Davis Jr. and so forth. And it became almost like a Coca Cola commercial — one more time. But Basie was very slick that way. And I guess I did learn something from him because I’m still around and I’m still doing it. But he was so natural man. What he did was so simple, everyone would think why didn’t I think of that, it was right in front of me? And so was Duke. All those guys were special breeds of people. A special breed I should say.
Well, fascinating. I really appreciate your time again. And I wish you the best in your travels, and all your projects, and your work with Jane.
